summary:
This project is an all-in-one Mars survival and navigation dashboard for astronauts in Gale Crater. It keeps missions safe using four simple features:
• Interactive Map Layers: Shows Blue (water ice), Black (dust traps), and Red (radiation) zones in real time.
• Astronaut Health & Base Panel: Tracks spacesuit dust wear, nuclear reactor power, and local weather/radiation risk scores.
• Biosafety Protocol: Locks restricted areas and limits tools to protect Mars from Earth bacteria.
• Orbit-to-Surface Security: Tracks space debris in Mars orbit to prevent crashes during landing and takeoff.
details:
1. What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

Our project is a real-time command, navigation, and survival dashboard developed for astronauts, rovers, and base systems operating on the Martian surface (specifically targeting challenging regions like Gale Crater). The system operates across three core layers:

  • Real-Time Map Layers: Maps the Martian terrain using interactive color-coded zones. Blue Zones indicate shallow water-ice deposits (30 cm below the surface) ideal for excavation, Black Zones mark loose dust traps where heavy vehicles risk sinking, and Red Zones highlight high cosmic radiation areas where exiting shelters is strictly prohibited.
  • Astronaut Health Bar & Base Telemetry: Continuously monitors spacesuit abrasion caused by glass-sharp Martian regolith dust (42% wear warning), the power level of the nuclear reactor supplying life support units (89% active), and a real-time dynamic regional risk score (75% dangerous) calculated from storms, temperature, and radiation data.
  • Two-Way Orbit-to-Surface Security: Integrates not only surface hazards but also defunct satellite debris drifting in Mars's orbit into the mapping system, eliminating collision risks from above during landing and takeoff operations.

2. What Are Its Benefits?

  • Eliminates Logistics Blindness: Prevents astronauts and autonomous rovers from getting trapped in loose dust or entering lethal radiation zones.
  • Optimizes Resource Efficiency: Pinpoints the closest subsurface water-ice deposits, saving critical time and energy during excavation and exploration missions.
  • Provides an Early Warning System: Consolidates vital metrics such as spacesuit wear and reactor power onto a single screen, enabling proactive intervention before equipment failure occurs.
  • Prevents Biological Contamination: Enforces Planetary Protection Protocols by restricting equipment usage in sensitive areas to prevent Earth-derived microorganisms from contaminating Mars's subsurface layers.

3. What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

The primary goal of the project is to maximize astronaut safety, reduce mission failure risks to zero, and close the "onboard computing gap" identified by NASA for 2026 in crewed Mars missions. Additionally, by protecting the Martian ecosystem from biological contamination, it ensures the scientific integrity and sustainability of future human settlements.

4. What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use?

  • Coding Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript were used to build the interactive dashboards, live telemetry simulations, and toggleable radar map interfaces.
  • Design & Presentation Software: Canva was used for UI/UX prototyping, visual layout design, and interactive widget integration.
  • Data & Reference Sources: NASA open datasets and mission reports served as the foundation for Gale Crater topography, regolith dust properties, planetary protection guidelines, and orbital debris risk models.

5. How Creative Is Your Project?

While existing space interfaces typically focus solely on surface navigation or isolated astronaut health metrics, our project unifies astronaut equipment telemetry, surface hazard mapping, planetary biosafety protocols, and orbital space debris tracking into a single integrated platform. Its "two-way orbit-to-surface security" approach and live interactive map layers set it apart from conventional mapping tools.

6. What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

While developing the project, our team (Ayşe Neva Yavruoğlu and Zehra Kul) carefully accounted for the following critical factors:

  • Physical & Environmental Hazards: Galactic cosmic rays, cryogenic freezing temperatures, severe dust storms, and the mechanical abrasiveness of sharp regolith dust.
  • Operational Safety: Orbital debris collision risks during landing and takeoff trajectories, as well as rover sinkage hazards in deep dust traps.
  • Ethical & Scientific Responsibility: Establishing dynamic buffer zones to protect potential habitable subsurface layers from terrestrial bacterial contamination.
  • User Experience (UX): Implementing high-contrast color coding (Blue, Black, Red) and simplified status bars so astronauts can read critical data within seconds during high-stress emergencies.
